question:
Let \[ z = \dfrac{1 + i}{\sqrt{2}}. \] What is

\[ \begin{aligned} &\left(z^{1^2} + z^{2^2} + z^{3^2} + \cdots + z^{12^2}\right) \\ &\quad {}\cdot \scriptsize \left(\dfrac{1}{z^{1^2}} + \dfrac{1}{z^{2^2}} + \dfrac{1}{z^{3^2}} + \cdots + \dfrac{1}{z^{12^2}}\right)? \end{aligned} \]
solution:
The powers of \(z\) repeat every eight exponents, so the large square exponents can be replaced by their remainders modulo \(8\). Indeed,
\[
z^2=\frac{(1+i)^2}{2}=i,\qquad z^4=-1,\qquad z^8=1.
\]
An odd square has remainder \(1\) modulo \(8\): writing the odd number as \(2r+1\), its square is \(4r(r+1)+1\), and \(r(r+1)\) is even. An even number not divisible by \(4\) has square congruent to \(4\) modulo \(8\), while a multiple of \(4\) has square divisible by \(8\).

These cases account for all twelve indices:

| Indices \(k\) | Number | \(k^2\bmod 8\) | \(z^{k^2}\) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| \(1,3,5,7,9,11\) | 6 | 1 | \(z\) |
| \(2,6,10\) | 3 | 4 | \(-1\) |
| \(4,8,12\) | 3 | 0 | \(1\) |

Thus the first parenthesized sum is
\[
6z+3(-1)+3(1)=6z.
\]
For the reciprocal sum, the six terms equal to \(z\) become \(1/z\), while \(1\) and \(-1\) are their own reciprocals. Therefore the second sum is \(6/z\), and the requested product is
\[
(6z)\left(\frac6z\right)=\boxed{36}.
\]
The answer is choice \(\mathrm{C}\).
